pos: adj. (secure from danger; preserved — in Scripture, never by circumstance but by a keeper)
etymology: Latin salvus, whole, unharmed — the same root as salvation. The Hebrew behind several occurrences is simply shalom, peace: to ask whether a man is safe is to ask whether it is peace with him.
biblical_def: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). Note the three parts: the tower is a name, not a place; the righteous must run, which is an act; and the safety is in the tower and not in the runner. The companion proverb gives the alternative: “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe” (Pro 29:25). A man is going to be governed either by what people may do to him or by God, and one of the two is a trap. Psalm 119 supplies the prayer: “Hold thou me up, and I shall be safe: and I will have respect unto thy statutes continually” (Psa 119:117) — the safety is God's holding, and the fruit of it is continual regard for His word. The saddest use of the word in Scripture is David's twice-asked question at the gate: “Is the young man Absalom safe?” (2Sa 18:29, 32) — a father asking after a son who had just tried to kill him, and the runner had to answer by describing his death without saying it. And the gladdest is the servant's report in the parable: “thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound” (Luk 15:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines safe as free from danger, secure from harm; and adds that no man is safe but he that is under the protection of God.
webster_full: SAFE, a. Free from danger of any kind; as safe from enemies; safe from disease.
1. Free from hurt, injury or damage; as, to bring goods safe to land.
2. Conferring safety; securing from harm; as a safe guide; a safe harbor.
SAFETY, n. Freedom from danger or hazard; exemption from hurt or loss.
scriptures: The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
Hold thou me up, and I shall be safe: and I will have respect unto thy statutes continually.
And he said unto him, Thy brother is come; and thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound.
corruption_summary: Safety has become the highest social good and the church's chief promise; Scripture makes it a name to run into, not a condition to be guaranteed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to treat safety as the supreme value, and its therapeutic form — the safe space, a room in which no one may be contradicted — is not a biblical category and should be refused as such. Scripture's promise is not a life without danger. Paul was beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and finally executed, and wrote from prison that the Lord shall deliver him from every evil work and preserve him unto His heavenly kingdom. The safety of Proverbs 18:10 is a tower, which implies a siege. It is where a man runs while the danger is real, and the thing that makes it safe is a name.

The second corruption is quieter and belongs to churches. Where the fear of man governs — of a congregation's reaction, of a donor, of the surrounding culture — the ministry becomes the management of risk, and Proverbs calls that a snare rather than a strategy. The alternative is not recklessness. It is that a man who has run into the tower has already lost the leverage that the fear of man depends on, and can therefore say what is true. Whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe is the only ground on which a preacher is free.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace, wholeness, welfare; sagab (H7682), to be set on high, inaccessible; migdal 'oz, a strong tower.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, soundness, welfare; 2 Samuel 18:29, 32 — literally, is there peace to the young man Absalom?
Hebrew sagab (H7682) — to be high, to be set on high out of reach; Proverbs 18:10, the righteous is set on high — safety by elevation, not by concealment.
Hebrew migdal 'oz (H4026, H5797) — a tower of strength; the figure for the name of the LORD.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to lean upon with confidence; Proverbs 29:25.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy, whole; Luke 15:27, received him safe and sound.
usage: “The righteous runneth into it, and is safe” — a tower implies a siege.
“The fear of man bringeth a snare” — and the alternative is trust.
“Is the young man Absalom safe?” — asked twice, of a son in rebellion.

pos: adj. (having great force or efficacy; in the Authorized Version, of the voice of the LORD, the word of God, and Paul's letters)
etymology: From power, Old French povoir, to be able. Three occurrences only, and it is worth noticing what Scripture calls powerful: a voice, a word, and some letters. Never an army.
biblical_def: “The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty” (Psa 29:4). The psalm is a thunderstorm: the voice breaks the cedars of Lebanon, divides the flames of fire, shakes the wilderness, makes the hinds to calve — and ends in the temple where every one speaks of His glory. God's power in Scripture is characteristically vocal. He spoke and it was done. The New Testament carries the same into the written word: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” (Heb 4:12). Quick means living. The word is not a record of God's past speech but an instrument presently in His hand, and its work is to divide what a man cannot divide in himself — to tell him which of his motives are actually his. The third use is the Corinthians' backhanded compliment: “his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible” (2Co 10:10). Paul quotes the insult against himself and does not deny the second half. God's power ran through an unimpressive man, which was Paul's whole argument.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines powerful as having great physical or moral power; forcible; efficacious; possessing energy or the power of producing great effects.
webster_full: POWERFUL, a. Having great physical or mechanical power; strong; forcible; mighty; as a powerful army.
1. Having great moral power; forcible to persuade the mind; as a powerful reason or argument.
2. Possessing great political and military power; as a powerful nation.
3. Efficacious; possessing or exerting great force or producing great effects.
scriptures: Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Psa 29:4
The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty.
For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.
corruption_summary: Power in ministry is sought in presence, technique and platform; Scripture attaches the word to a voice, a text, and a man they thought unimpressive.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary church largely locates power in the visible: personality, production, technique, the size of a following. Scripture calls three things powerful, and all three are verbal — the LORD's voice, the written word, and a set of letters from a man his critics found weak in person and contemptible in speech. Paul's response to the taunt is the whole doctrine: he does not argue that he is really impressive; he says the weapons of his warfare are not carnal but mighty through God, and elsewhere that he came in weakness and fear and much trembling that your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.

Hebrews 4:12 must also be rescued from being quoted as an advertisement. It is not a slogan about the Bible's usefulness; it is a warning inside an argument about entering God's rest, and its work is surgical. The word divides soul from spirit and discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart, and the next verse says all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do. That is the power the church actually needs and most often avoids: a word that tells a man the truth about his own motives before it comforts him.
roots_summary: Greek energes (G1756), active, effective, at work; zon (G2198), living, quick; Hebrew koach (H3581), strength, power.
roots_lines: Greek energes (G1756) — active, operative, effectual; Hebrews 4:12, and the root of our energy — the word is at work, not merely capable.
Greek zon (G2198) — living; Hebrews 4:12, rendered quick — the word of God is alive.
Greek tomoteros (G5114) — sharper, more cutting; sharper than any twoedged sword.
Greek kritikos (G2924) — able to judge, discerning; a discerner of the thoughts and intents.
Hebrew koach (H3581) — strength, ability, power; Psalm 29:4, the voice of the LORD is in power.
usage: “The word of God is quick, and powerful” — living, and at work.
“The voice of the LORD is powerful” — and it breaks the cedars.
“His letters… are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak”.

pos: adv. and adj. (kindly; in the Hebrew idiom, to the heart — speaking so as to reach a person's heart)
etymology: From friend, Saxon freond, one who loves. The Hebrew phrase behind two of the three occurrences is 'al leb, literally upon the heart: to speak friendly is to speak to somebody's heart, comfortably and to the point of need.
biblical_def: Ruth names what Boaz did for her: “Let me find favour in thy sight, my lord; for that thou hast comforted me, and for that thou hast spoken friendly unto thine handmaid, though I be not like unto one of thine handmaidens” (Rut 2:13). The Hebrew is thou hast spoken to the heart of thine handmaid — the same idiom used when God says He will allure Israel into the wilderness and speak comfortably unto her. A Moabite widow gleaning at the edge of a field was addressed as a person, and it changed her life and, through her, the line of David. Judges 19 uses the same phrase for a husband who went after his estranged concubine “to speak friendly unto her, and to bring her again” (Jdg 19:3) — the chapter that follows is one of the darkest in Scripture, and the tenderness of that opening line makes the horror worse rather than better. And Proverbs gives the plain maxim: “A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother” (Pro 18:24). Friendship in Scripture is a duty before it is a feeling — a man must shew himself friendly — and behind every human friendship stands the one that sticks closer than blood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines friendly as having the temper and disposition of a friend, kind, favorable, disposed to promote the good of another.
webster_full: FRIENDLY, a. Having the temper and disposition of a friend; kind; favorable; disposed to promote the good of another.
1. Disposed to peace; not hostile.
2. Favorable; propitious; salutary; promoting the good of; as a friendly breeze.
FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection.
scriptures: Rut 2:13

Then she said, Let me find favour in thy sight, my lord; for that thou hast comforted me, and for that thou hast spoken friendly unto thine handmaid, though I be not like unto one of thine handmaidens.
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Jdg 19:3

And her husband arose, and went after her, to speak friendly unto her, and to bring her again, having his servant with him, and a couple of asses: and she brought him into her father's house: and when the father of the damsel saw him, he rejoiced to meet him.
corruption_summary: Friendliness is treated as a temperament some have and others lack; Proverbs makes it something a man shows on purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern speech classifies friendliness as a personality trait — some are outgoing, some are not, and little is owed either way. Proverbs 18:24 makes it an act of will: a man that hath friends must shew himself friendly. The showing comes first. This is the same logic by which Scripture commands love, which cannot be commanded if it is only a feeling but can be commanded if it is chiefly a settled willing of another's good. The introvert is not excused and the extrovert is not congratulated; both are told to show something.

The Hebrew idiom is worth keeping in the ear, because it corrects the shallow sense of the English. To speak friendly is to speak to the heart — not chatter, not pleasantry, but words aimed at where a person actually lives. Boaz spoke to a foreign widow's heart and named exactly what she had done and under whose wings she had come to trust. God uses the same phrase of Himself in Hosea 2:14. And the proverb ends where it must: there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother — the One who called His disciples friends on the night He was betrayed, and then laid down His life for them.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'al leb — upon the heart, the idiom rendered friendly; re'a (H7453), a friend, a neighbour; dabaq (H1692), to cleave.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar 'al leb — to speak upon the heart; Ruth 2:13, Judges 19:3, Genesis 34:3, Isaiah 40:2 (speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem), Hosea 2:14.
Hebrew re'a (H7453) — a friend, companion, neighbour; Proverbs 18:24, and Exodus 33:11, the LORD spake unto Moses as a man speaketh unto his friend.
Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cleave, to stick fast; the friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Hebrew 'oheb (H157) — one who loves; the participle behind Abraham, the friend of God (2Ch 20:7; Jas 2:23).
Greek philos (G5384) — a friend, one dearly loved; John 15:13-15, greater love hath no man than this.
usage: “Thou hast spoken friendly unto thine handmaid” — to her heart.
“A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly” — the showing comes first.
“A friend that sticketh closer than a brother”.

pos: adj. (not hard; and, of a yoke, well-fitting — kind rather than light)
etymology: Old French aisié, at ease. The Greek behind our Lord's my yoke is easy is chrestos — kindly, serviceable, good — the same word rendered kind and gracious elsewhere. The yoke is not weightless; it is well made and does not gall.
biblical_def: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Mat 11:30). A yoke is a working harness, and our Lord is inviting men to take one on, not to lay one down: take my yoke upon you, and learn of me. The Greek word is chrestos, elsewhere translated kind and good; the picture is of a yoke shaped to the animal so that it does not chafe. The rest He promises is found under a yoke, not away from it, and the contrast is with the burdens grievous to be borne that the scribes laid on men's shoulders and would not touch with a finger. James uses the same root for wisdom from above: it is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated” (Jas 3:17) — approachable, open to persuasion, but pure first, so that the openness is never at truth's expense. Paul uses the word for plain speech in the assembly: “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). And Proverbs marks who finds knowledge easy: “A scorner seeketh wisdom, and findeth it not: but knowledge is easy unto him that understandeth” (Pro 14:6). The scorner comes to mock and finds nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines easy as being at rest, free from pain or anxiety; not difficult, requiring no great labor; and of manners, ready, not constrained.
webster_full: EASY, a. Quiet; being at rest; free from pain, disturbance or annoyance.
1. Free from anxiety, care, solicitude; tranquil; as an easy mind.
2. Giving no pain or disturbance; as an easy posture.
3. Not difficult; that gives or requires no great labor or effort.
4. Complying; ready to accommodate; yielding to the will of others.
scriptures: For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
Jas 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Pro 14:6
A scorner seeketh wisdom, and findeth it not: but knowledge is easy unto him that understandeth.
corruption_summary: “My yoke is easy” is preached as a promise of an undemanding Christianity; the sentence begins with take my yoke upon you.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 11:30 has been made the charter of an easy-believism our Lord never offered. He is speaking to men labouring and heavy laden under the scribes' burdens and offering an exchange, not an exemption: take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. Two verses later in Luke's parallel material He tells the multitudes to count the cost, and elsewhere to take up the cross daily. The yoke is easy because the One who made it is kind and because He is in it with us, not because there is nothing to draw.

James 3:17 guards the other flank, and its order should be preached as it stands. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable. Every generation is tempted to reverse those two, buying peace at the price of purity and calling the result gentleness. The same verse ends without partiality, and without hypocrisy, which means an openness to persuasion that is genuine and not a technique. A man easy to be intreated is not a man easily moved off the truth; he is a man you can actually talk to about it.
roots_summary: Greek chrestos (G5543), kind, good, serviceable — of the yoke; eupeithes (G2138), easily persuaded; eusemos (G2154), well-marked, clear in meaning.
roots_lines: Greek chrestos (G5543) — kind, gracious, serviceable, well-fitted; Matthew 11:30, and Luke 6:35, He is kind unto the unthankful.
Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke; the working harness our Lord offers, and Galatians 5:1, the yoke of bondage He does not.
Greek eupeithes (G2138) — easily persuaded, compliant, open to reason; James 3:17 — its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek eusemos (G2154) — well-marked, distinct, easy to understand; 1 Corinthians 14:9.
Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, chaste; James 3:17, the first quality of heavenly wisdom.
usage: “My yoke is easy” — and it is still a yoke.
“First pure, then peaceable… and easy to be intreated” — in that order.
“Words easy to be understood… else ye shall speak into the air”.

pos: adj. (suitable, qualified, proper for a purpose)
etymology: Of uncertain origin, meaning apt or suited. The Authorized Version uses it for men fit for war, a man fit to lead the scapegoat away, conduct fit in the Lord, and the solemn negative — not fit for the kingdom of God.
biblical_def: The most searching use is our Lord's: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:62). The image is exact — a ploughman who turns his head cuts a crooked furrow — and it was said to a man whose request was entirely reasonable: let me first go bid them farewell at home. Divided attention, not open rebellion, is what unfits him. On the Day of Atonement the live goat was sent away “by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness” (Lev 16:21), bearing all the iniquities of Israel upon his head into a land not inhabited. The Hebrew margin reads a man of opportunity, a man ready and appointed for it. Chronicles uses the word of David's Gadites, “men of war fit for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces were like the faces of lions” (1Ch 12:8). Proverbs applies it to the order of a young man's life: “Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house” (Pro 24:27) — field before house, provision before establishment. And Paul uses it of the creational order in the home: “Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord” (Col 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fit as suitable, convenient, meet, becoming; and qualified, competent, prepared for a purpose.
webster_full: FIT, a. Suitable; convenient; meet; becoming.
1. Qualified; as, a man is fit for an office.
2. Prepared; ready.
FIT, v.t. To adapt; to suit; to make suitable.
FITNESS, n. Suitableness; adaptedness; propriety.
scriptures: Luk 9:62
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.

And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins, putting them upon the head of the goat, and shall send him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness:
Col 3:18
Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord.
Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house.
corruption_summary: “As it is fit in the Lord” is treated as a cultural leftover; Paul grounds the household order in creation, not in custom.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 3:18 is regularly explained away as first-century household convention that the gospel has since dissolved. The explanation cannot survive the way the apostles actually argue. Paul grounds headship in the creation order, not in Roman custom — for Adam was first formed, then Eve (1Ti 2:13) — and in the relation of Christ to the church (Eph 5:22-33), which is not a cultural arrangement. Peter appeals to Sarah, centuries before any Greco-Roman code (1Pe 3:5-6). And the same passages bind the husband to a love measured by Christ's giving of Himself, which no surrounding culture had ever required. What Scripture calls fit in the Lord is an ordered mutual self-giving, and it is neither the tyranny it is caricatured as nor the interchangeability offered in its place.

The second thing to hold is Luke 9:62, which is the sharpest word in the entry. The man who was refused had asked to say goodbye to his family. Nothing in the request was wicked; it simply revealed a divided heart at the moment of call. A ploughman looking back leaves a crooked furrow, and the kingdom is not served by men whose attention is behind them. This is not a doctrine of sinless devotion — Peter looked back, wept, and was restored — but it is a refusal to enlist anyone on the understanding that Christ may have what is left over.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'itti (H6261), timely, ready, appointed — the fit man of Leviticus 16; 'arak (H6186), to set in order; Greek euthetos (G2111), well-placed, fit for use.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'itti (H6261) — timely, ready, appointed for the occasion; Leviticus 16:21, the fit man who led away the scapegoat — its only occurrence.
Hebrew 'azazel (H5799) — the scapegoat, the goat of departure; the live goat that bore the iniquities away.
Greek euthetos (G2111) — well-placed, useful, fit; Luke 9:62, 14:35, Hebrews 6:7.
Greek aroton / arotron (G723) — a plough; Luke 9:62, the only New Testament occurrence.
Greek aneko (G433) — to be proper, becoming, fitting; Colossians 3:18, Ephesians 5:4, Philemon 8.
usage: “Having put his hand to the plough, and looking back” — a crooked furrow.
“By the hand of a fit man into the wilderness” — a man appointed for it.
“Prepare thy work without… and afterwards build thine house”.

pos: adj. (successful; going well — in the Authorized Version, chiefly of a journey and of a man with whom God is)
etymology: Latin prosperus, favourable, from pro spe, according to hope. The biblical uses are dominated by the idea of a way or journey that succeeds, and the question the servant of Abraham asked at the well — whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous.
biblical_def: “And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian” (Gen 39:2). The sentence is the key to the word, and its setting is decisive: Joseph is a slave. Sold by his brothers, in a foreign house, and Scripture calls him prosperous — because the LORD was with him, which is what the word actually reports. Within a few verses he is in prison, and the same phrase follows him there. Joshua receives the classic promise: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success” (Jos 1:8). Note the chain — the book in the mouth, meditation day and night, observance to do, and then the prospering. Abraham's servant wonders at Rebekah, holding his peace, “to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not” (Gen 24:21). Isaiah uses it of Cyrus, a pagan king: “I have called him: I have brought him, and he shall make his way prosperous” (Isa 48:15). And Paul asks for a prosperous journey to Rome “by the will of God” (Rom 1:10) — and got there in chains, shipwrecked on the way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prosperous as advancing in the pursuit of any thing desirable; successful; and favorable, as a prosperous wind or voyage.
webster_full: PROSPEROUS, a. Advancing in the pursuit of any thing desirable; making gain or increase; thriving; successful.
1. Favorable; favoring success; as a prosperous wind.
PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed.
PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise.
scriptures: Gen 39:2
And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
Jos 1:8

This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.
Rom 1:10
Making request, if by any means now at length I might have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come unto you.
I, even I, have spoken; yea, I have called him: I have brought him, and he shall make his way prosperous.
corruption_summary: Joshua 1:8 is preached as a formula for material increase; the word's clearest instance is a slave in a foreign house.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching — and the softer version of it that circulates in ordinary evangelical churches — treats Joshua 1:8 as a transaction: meditate on the word and God will make you materially successful. Two things are wrong with it. First, the prospering promised to Joshua concerns the specific commission he was given, the conquest of Canaan, and is conditioned on doing all that is written in the law. Second, the word's own showcase is Genesis 39:2, where a prosperous man describes a slave with no wages, no freedom and no prospects, and the reason given is that the LORD was with Joseph. Biblical prosperity is the presence of God in a man's appointed place, and Scripture is willing to use the word of a prison.

Paul's prayer supplies the discipline. He asked for a prosperous journey to Rome by the will of God, and the answer came by way of a riot, two years' imprisonment at Caesarea, an appeal to Caesar, a shipwreck and a viper. He arrived, and he arrived a prisoner, and from that house he wrote the letters we still read. Prayer for prosperity is entirely lawful; Paul prayed it. But it is prayed under the will of God, and the answer may be a chain that turns out to have been the shortest road.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsalach (H6743), to advance, to succeed, to prosper; sakal (H7919), to act wisely and so to prosper; Greek euodoo (G2137), to have a good journey.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to push forward, to advance, to prosper; Genesis 24:21, 39:2, Joshua 1:8, Isaiah 48:15.
Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be prudent, to act wisely, and so to have good success; Joshua 1:8, the margin reads do wisely.
Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to mutter, to meditate; Joshua 1:8, Psalm 1:2 — meditation in Scripture is spoken under the breath.
Greek euodoo (G2137) — to be led along a good road, to have a prosperous journey; Romans 1:10, 1 Corinthians 16:2, 3 John 2.
Greek thelema theou (G2307) — the will of God; the condition Paul attached to his request.
usage: “The LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man” — in a slave's house.
“Then thou shalt make thy way prosperous” — after the book, the meditation, the doing.
“A prosperous journey by the will of God” — and he came in chains.

pos: adv. (wonderfully; in a manner exciting astonishment)
etymology: From marvel, Latin mirari, to wonder at. Three occurrences: God thunders marvellously, a king is marvellously helped, and a prophet's hearers are told to wonder marvellously at a work they will not believe.
biblical_def: Elihu says of the storm, “God thundereth marvellously with his voice; great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend” (Job 37:5). The point is not merely that God is loud but that His works exceed comprehension, and that this is a reason for worship rather than a defect in the evidence. Habakkuk carries it into history, and God says the astonishing thing Himself: “Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be told you” (Hab 1:5). The work was the raising up of the Chaldeans — God answering a prophet's complaint about Judah's wickedness by sending a worse nation to judge her. Paul quotes this verse at Antioch as a warning to despisers (Act 13:41). God's marvellous works are not always the ones we would have chosen. And Chronicles applies the adverb to a man, with a warning attached that has become proverbial: Uzziah built engines on the towers of Jerusalem, “And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong” (2Ch 26:15). Till he was strong — and the next verse says that when he was strong his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he went into the temple to burn incense and came out a leper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines marvellously as in a manner to excite wonder or surprise; wonderfully; strangely.
webster_full: MARVELLOUSLY, adv. In a manner to excite wonder or surprise; wonderfully; strangely.
MARVELLOUS, a. Wonderful; strange; exciting wonder or some degree of surprise.
1. Surpassing credit; incredible.
MARVEL, n. A wonder; something that arrests the attention and causes a person to stand or gaze, or to pause.
scriptures: Hab 1:5
Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be told you.
Job 37:5
God thundereth marvellously with his voice; great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend.

And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men, to be on the towers and upon the bulwarks, to shoot arrows and great stones withal. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong.
corruption_summary: Divine help is read as divine approval of the helped man; Uzziah was marvellously helped till he was strong, and strength ruined him.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 26:15 contains four of the most sobering words in the historical books: till he was strong. Uzziah was genuinely helped by God — the fortifications, the army, the engines, the wells, the wide fame were all a gift, and Scripture says so plainly. And the gift became the occasion of his ruin, because he read God's help as a verdict on himself. The pattern is common enough to be a rule: men fall not at the bottom but at the top, and the ministry, the business or the reputation that God built becomes the reason its holder thinks himself entitled to the priest's censer. He died a leper in a several house.

Habakkuk supplies the corrective to a related error — the assumption that God's marvellous works will be recognizable as good to the people they happen to. I will work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be told you, and the work was Babylon. Job's Elihu says the same in the register of nature: great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend. A God whose works we could always audit would be a God our size. The believer's business is not to approve the providence but to trust the character, which is why Habakkuk ends where he does: yet I will rejoice in the LORD.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamah (H8539), to be astounded; pala' (H6381), to be wonderful, beyond ability; chazaq (H2388), to be or become strong.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamah (H8539) — to be amazed, astounded; Habakkuk 1:5, wonder marvellously — the verb doubled for emphasis.
Hebrew pala' (H6381) — to be extraordinary, beyond one's power; Job 37:5, and Genesis 18:14, is any thing too hard for the LORD?
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen; 2 Chronicles 26:15-16, marvellously helped till he was strong, and then his heart was lifted up.
Hebrew gabahh leb — the heart lifted up; the phrase for the pride that destroyed Uzziah.
Greek thaumazo (G2296) — to marvel, to wonder; Acts 13:41, where Paul quotes Habakkuk against the despisers.
usage: “Wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days” — and it was Babylon.
“God thundereth marvellously with his voice” — and we cannot comprehend it.
“He was marvellously helped, till he was strong”.

pos: adv. (in a manner exciting terror; dreadfully)
etymology: Latin terrere, to frighten. In the Authorized Version the adverb belongs almost entirely to one image, repeated twice in a single chapter of Isaiah: the LORD arising to shake terribly the earth, and men going into the holes of the rocks.
biblical_def: Twice in one chapter Isaiah paints the same scene, and the repetition is deliberate: “they shall go into the holes of the rocks, and into the caves of the earth, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth” (Isa 2:19), and again, “To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks… when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth” (Isa 2:21). The chapter has been levelling everything men lift up — the cedars of Lebanon, the high towers, the ships of Tarshish, the lofty looks — and this is the end of it: the idols cast to the moles and the bats, and their owners hiding in the rocks. Revelation 6:15-16 takes up the identical picture for the day of the Lamb's wrath, kings and great men and every bondman calling for the rocks to fall on them. The third occurrence is Nahum's description of the assault on Nineveh: “the chariots shall be with flaming torches in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken” (Nah 2:3). The adverb is reserved in Scripture for what happens when God rises. He is not described as terrible in His ordinary dealings with His people, and the whole of the gospel is that the man who has fled to Christ has no reason to look for a rock to hide under.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines terribly as in a manner to excite terror; dreadfully; violently; and terrible as adapted to excite terror, awful, formidable.
webster_full: TERRIBLY, adv. In a manner to excite terror or fright; dreadfully; formidably.
1. Violently; very greatly.
TERRIBLE, a. Frightful; adapted to excite terror; dreadful; formidable.
1. Adapted to impress dread, awe or solemnity; as the terrible majesty of God.
scriptures: Isa 2:19
And they shall go into the holes of the rocks, and into the caves of the earth, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth.
Isa 2:21
To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth.
Nah 2:3
The shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men are in scarlet: the chariots shall be with flaming torches in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken.
corruption_summary: The terror of God is edited out as unworthy of Him; Isaiah says men will hide in the rocks from the glory of His majesty.
corruption_paragraphs: A God who is never terrible is a God who has been reduced to a friend, and the reduction is now nearly complete in popular religion. Isaiah 2 will not allow it: men go into holes in the ground for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, and the glory and the terror are named in the same breath because they are the same thing seen by a creature not reconciled to it. The New Testament does not soften this; Revelation repeats the picture, and Hebrews says our God is a consuming fire in a sentence about serving Him acceptably with reverence and godly fear.

But the doctrine is not preached rightly if it stops there, and the Reformed tradition has always insisted on the second half. The believer's relation to that same majesty is adoption: ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The terror is real, it is deserved, and it has been borne. The man who has fled to Christ is not looking for a rock to fall on him, because the Rock has already been struck for him. Preach the terror to establish the refuge; preach the refuge so the terror does not crush.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'arats (H6206), to terrify, to shake with terror; ga'on (H1347), majesty, excellency; pachad (H6343), dread.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'arats (H6206) — to cause to tremble, to terrify; Isaiah 2:19, 2:21, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth.
Hebrew pachad (H6343) — dread, terror; Isaiah 2:19, for fear of the LORD.
Hebrew hadar ge'ono — the glory of his majesty; the second reason men hide, set beside the first.
Hebrew ra'al (H7477) — to shake, to reel; Nahum 2:3, the fir trees terribly shaken.
Greek phoberos (G5398) — fearful, terrible; Hebrews 10:31, 12:21, and 12:29, our God is a consuming fire.
usage: “When he ariseth to shake terribly the earth” — twice in one chapter.
“For fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty” — one thing, two names.
“The fir trees shall be terribly shaken” — the day of his preparation.

pos: adv. (after the manner of the Spirit; by the Spirit's enabling — and once, figuratively)
etymology: From spiritual, Latin spiritualis. In the New Testament the adverb marks the mode in which a thing is minded, discerned or named — and the three occurrences give a mind, a faculty, and a figure.
biblical_def: “For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace” (Rom 8:6). Paul is not distinguishing two temperaments but two natures — the flesh and the Spirit — and the words are absolute: death on one side, life and peace on the other. The next verse explains why there is no middle ground: the carnal mind is enmity against God, for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. The second occurrence supplies the epistemology: “the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned” (1Co 2:14). The unregenerate man's difficulty with Scripture is not first intellectual but constitutional; he lacks the faculty, as a blind man lacks the organ for colour, and the remedy is not better argument but the new birth. This is the doctrine of total depravity applied to the mind, and it is why every Reformed doctrine of preaching depends on the Spirit rather than on rhetoric. The third occurrence is different in kind: the great city where the two witnesses lie dead, “which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified” (Rev 11:8) — a place named not by geography but by character.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spiritually as without corporeal grossness or sensuality, in a manner conformed to the spirit; and with attention to things of the spirit.
webster_full: SPIRITUALLY, adv. Without corporeal grossness or sensuality; in a manner conformed to the spirit or soul.
1. With attention to things of the spirit; with a spiritual mind.
SPIRITUAL, a. Consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal.
2. Mental; intellectual; as spiritual armor.
3. Not gross; refined from external things; not sensual; relative to mind only.
scriptures: Rom 8:6
For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Rev 11:8
And their dead bodies shall lie in the street of the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified.
corruption_summary: “Spirituality” has become a contentless good detached from the Holy Ghost; Paul makes the word mean the mind governed by the Spirit of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern noun spirituality names a vague inwardness with no object — a person may be spiritual and believe nothing in particular. The New Testament adverb is the opposite of vague: it means by the Holy Spirit, and it is used to divide the human race in two. To be spiritually minded is life and peace; to be carnally minded is death. There is no third category of the religiously inclined. A man is indwelt by the Spirit of Christ or he is none of His (Rom 8:9), and the sincerity of his spiritual interest does not alter which side of that line he is on.

1 Corinthians 2:14 has a direct consequence for how the church works. If the natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit because he lacks the faculty, then no amount of persuasion, atmosphere or argument will produce a convert; only the sovereign work of regeneration will. That does not make preaching unnecessary — it is the appointed means, and faith cometh by hearing — but it does end the manipulation. The preacher states the truth plainly and prays for the Spirit to open eyes, because he knows exactly what he cannot do.
roots_summary: Greek pneumatikos (G4153), spiritually, by the Spirit; psuchikos (G5591), natural, soulish; phronema (G5427), the mind, the bent of thought.
roots_lines: Greek pneumatikos (G4153) — spiritually, in a spiritual manner; 1 Corinthians 2:14, Revelation 11:8 — its only two occurrences as an adverb.
Greek psuchikos (G5591) — natural, of the soul as opposed to the Spirit; 1 Corinthians 2:14, 15:44, Jude 19.
Greek phronema (G5427) — the mind, the way of thinking, the bent; Romans 8:6-7, the mind of the flesh and the mind of the Spirit.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to discern, to judge; 1 Corinthians 2:14, spiritually discerned.
Greek dechomai (G1209) — to receive, to welcome; the natural man receiveth not — not a failure of intellect but a refusal of welcome.
usage: “To be spiritually minded is life and peace” — and there is no third option.
“Because they are spiritually discerned” — the faculty is missing, not the argument.
“Which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt” — named by character.

pos: v. (to free, to deliver out of the hand of another; to clear away)
etymology: Old Norse rydja, to clear. In the Authorized Version rid is a rescue word: to rid a man is to get him out of somebody's hand, and the phrase that follows it is nearly always out of the hand of.
biblical_def: The word's great occurrence is in the second of the four great I wills of the exodus: “I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments” (Exo 6:6). Bring out, rid, redeem — three stages of one deliverance, and every verb has God for its subject. The passover cups of the Jewish seder were built on these promises. Reuben uses the word for a rescue he intended and did not carry out: “Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit… that he might rid him out of their hands, to deliver him to his father again” (Gen 37:22). Reuben meant well, acted by half measures, and came back to an empty pit. Good intentions that avoid confrontation usually arrive too late. Psalm 82 makes it a command to judges: “Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked” (Psa 82:4) — the magistrate's office is defined by whose hand he takes people out of. David prays it for himself twice in one psalm: “Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters” (Psa 144:7). And Leviticus promises it of the land itself: “I will rid evil beasts out of the land” (Lev 26:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rid as to free, to deliver; to set free, to release; and to drive away, to remove by violence.
webster_full: RID, v.t. To free; to deliver; as, to rid one from his troubles.
1. To separate; to drive away.
2. To free; to clear; to disencumber; as, to rid the house of vermin.
3. To dispatch. I will rid you out of their bondage. Exodus 6.
RIDDANCE, n. Deliverance; a setting free.
scriptures: Exo 6:6

Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:
Psa 82:4
Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.
And Reuben said unto them, Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit that is in the wilderness, and lay no hand upon him; that he might rid him out of their hands, to deliver him to his father again.
Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children;
corruption_summary: Deliverance is described as self-liberation; every biblical use of this verb puts the rescue in another's hand.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing story of the age is self-liberation: a person frees himself, throws off what binds him, and becomes what he chooses. Every occurrence of this verb in Scripture describes the opposite grammar. I will bring you out… I will rid you… I will redeem you — four times God is the subject and Israel is the object, and Israel's contribution to the exodus was to be too weak to leave. The gospel keeps the same structure: men are delivered from the power of darkness and translated into the kingdom of God's dear Son, and the verbs belong to God.

Reuben is the cautionary figure, and he is more familiar than we like. He genuinely intended to save Joseph, he opposed the murder, and he arranged a half measure that would let him rescue the boy later without confronting his brothers now. He came back and the pit was empty, and he rent his clothes and said whither shall I go? Half measures to avoid confrontation are a common form of cowardice among decent men, and they characteristically produce grief rather than safety. Psalm 82 tells the man with authority to do the harder thing: rid them out of the hand of the wicked — which requires taking hold.
roots_summary: Hebrew natsal (H5337), to snatch away, to deliver; ga'al (H1350), to redeem as a kinsman; shabath (H7673), to cause to cease.
roots_lines: Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to strip away, to snatch out of the hand of, to deliver; Exodus 6:6, Psalm 82:4, 144:7, 144:11.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to act as kinsman, to redeem; the third verb of Exodus 6:6, I will redeem you.
Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, to cause to cease; Leviticus 26:6, I will rid evil beasts out of the land.
Hebrew yad (H3027) — hand; the standing idiom — delivered out of the hand of.
Greek rhuomai (G4506) — to draw to oneself, to rescue; Matthew 6:13, deliver us from evil; Colossians 1:13.
usage: “I will rid you out of their bondage” — the second of the four I wills.
“Rid them out of the hand of the wicked” — the magistrate's office defined.
“That he might rid him out of their hands” — and Reuben came back to an empty pit.
